«единичка».finding: At Leningrad/St Petersburg Physics-Mathematics Lyceum No. 239 — Perelman's and Smirnov's school — each year-group is split into numbered classes (10-1, 10-2, and so on), and the lyceum's own olympiad rosters still label pupils that way. Kononov's text says the school 'recruited' Nikolai Durov into the famous «единичка», the special class of olympiad medallists, and that the first two classes of every year, «единичку» и «двойку», were where the geniuses were gathered. So «единичка» and «двойка» here are affectionate diminutives naming class 1 and class 2, insider school slang roughly equivalent to 'the One' and 'the Two', and they carry prestige: for a Russian reader of 2013, being in the 239 «единичка» signals the top of the country's mathematical talent pipeline, together with the brutal training regime Kononov describes (nervous breakdowns over unsolved problems). The trap is that «двойка» in ordinary school Russian is the failing mark on the five-point scale, so a careless translator turns a pair of elite class names into grades; nothing here refers to marks.

https://www.lektorium.tv/university/17060 (profile of Presidential FML No. 239: 60+ international olympiad winners, Perelman, Smirnov)

rendering.en: the 'One' — Class 1, School 239's top stream (paired with the 'Two')
rendering.zh: “一班”（239中学的尖子班，与“二班”并称）

«единичка».rationale: I keep the denotation (a numbered class, so the «единичка»/«двойка» pair survives) and the prestige connotation via a first-mention gloss, sacrificing the warmth of the Russian diminutive; Chinese 一班 carries the top-class connotation on its own, while English and Japanese need the gloss because a numbered class implies no ranking there.

вертикаль власти.finding: A fixed Russian political term for the top-down chain of executive authority running from the president down through the regions. The phrase circulated in the press from the early 1990s and Primakov used «вертикаль исполнительной власти» in January 1999, but it became Putin's own programmatic slogan from 2000: «укрепление вертикали власти» names a concrete package — the seven federal districts with presidential plenipotentiaries (decree 849 of May 2000), the reform of the Federation Council, and the abolition of direct gubernatorial elections in 2004. By 2013 it had drifted from official self-description to worn journalistic shorthand, and in liberal writing it is used metonymically for the regime itself as something one does not cross. That is exactly Kononov's use: businessmen living through «эпоху мелкотемья и боязни не угодить вертикали власти» — fear of displeasing the vertical, treated as an actor rather than a structure. English, Chinese and Japanese all have settled equivalents in writing on Russia, so this should be a lookup rather than a fresh coinage.

вертикаль власти.rationale: In English and Chinese I keep denotation, the vertical metaphor and recognisability together, because 'the power vertical' and 「权力垂直体系」 are both what specialist writing already uses; on first mention I would attach 'Putin's' and 「普京的」 so a reader with no Russian context knows it names a specific system rather than a general observation about hierarchy. Japanese is the one real trade: I drop the literal calque 「権力の垂直」, which a Japanese reader will not recognise as a term of art, in favour of the National Diet Library's 「垂直的権力構造」, which buys recognisability and denotation at the cost of the compact metaphor and of the tired, faintly sardonic edge the phrase had acquired in Russian by 2013 — that edge has to be carried by the surrounding sentence in all three languages.

дом Зингера.finding: Nevsky Prospekt 28, built 1902–04 by Pavel Suzor as the Russian headquarters of the American Singer sewing-machine company — «Зингер» is simply Singer in Cyrillic. Its glass globe on a corner turret was Suzor's dodge around the ban on building higher than 23.5 metres on Nevsky, and it faces the Kazan Cathedral, which is the view from the negotiating room in the prologue. Nationalised in 1919, it housed the state publishers, Marshak's Detgiz and the children's journals «Чиж» and «Ёж», and a whole wing of the censorship committee; from 1938 Petersburgers have equally called it «Дом книги» after the bookshop, so the building carries two live names at once. VK took floors here around 2008–2010 (ru.wikipedia dates the seventh-floor lease to 2010, CNews says the headquarters was there from 2008), and Kononov uses «дом Зингера» throughout as metonymy for the company itself, the way one says 'Redmond'. The prologue's small mystery — a wrought-iron panel naming the first owner, printed in Latin as Zinger — is one an English reader cannot have, because 'Singer' gives the game away at once.

дом Зингера.rationale: I keep the company link visible in all three languages rather than the Russian sound: 'Singer House' is the standard English name, 胜家 is the established Chinese name of the Singer brand, and シンガーハウス is what Japanese coverage uses — so I preserve denotation and the sewing-machine irony (a nerd commune in a Victorian sales office) and give up the prologue's brief withholding, which is unrecoverable and should not be faked by transliterating 'Zinger'. Two riders: in Chinese avoid the purely phonetic 辛格大厦, which severs the link to the sewing machines, and 胜家公司楼 is the Wikipedia headword if a publisher prefers it; and «Дом книги» needs its own fixed rendering — the House of Books / 书籍之家 / 「本の家」（ドム・クニーギ） — since one building answers to two names in the same book.

«Желания».finding: A real VKontakte feature, launched July 2010 as a joint project with OZON.ru — the 'сильнейший интернет-торговец страны' the unnamed expat in the prologue runs. It is a gift wishlist, not a gift shop: a «Хочу в подарок» button on the retailer's product pages pushed an item into the «Желания» section of the user's VK page, where friends could see it and club together to buy it with VK's internal currency, the голоса. Russian press of the time also called it «Мои желания», and VK's press chief Vladislav Tsyplukhin said publicly in 2010 that the commission was hundredths of one per cent, non-zero only because Russian law forbade a zero rate — which sits oddly beside the prologue's shouting match over five, ten and twenty per cent, and is worth knowing before a translator smooths the scene. For a Russian reader in 2013 the word carried no glamour: it was a plain UI label, and the point of the scene is that Durov treats a near-zero-margin feature as a matter of principle. The name is descriptive, not a coined brand like Telegram, so it can be translated — but once, and then left alone.
sources: https://www.seonews.ru/events/vkontakte-i-ozonru-ispolnyayut-jelaniya/ (July 2010, VK + OZON.ru launch, «Хочу в подарок» button)
https://roem.ru/29-07-2010/120886/v-kontakte-sdelal-svoy-market/ (Durov in the comments on the Merchant API and zero commission)
https://www.retail.ru/news/odnoklassniki-kooperiruyutsya-s-internet-magazinami/ (Tsyplukhin: commission of hundredths of a per cent; service called «Мои желания»)
https://www.litres.ru/book/nikolay-kononov-2/kod-durova-realnaya-istoriya-vkontakte-i-ee-sozdatelya-4442369/chitat-onlayn/ (prologue text as published)
«Желания».rationale: For English and Chinese I keep the literal name — the Russian is simply the plural noun 'wishes', and both 'Wishes' and “心愿” work as a feature label, with a first-use gloss ('Wishes, VKontakte's gift-wishlist service' / “心愿”——VKontakte 的礼物心愿单功能) doing the explaining, so I preserve denotation and the flat corporate register and give up only instant self-evidence. Japanese is where I break the pattern deliberately: 「ウィッシュ」 renders the English rather than the Russian and reads as a fragment, while a literal 「願いごと」 pulls towards tanabata-style wishes, so I take 「ウィッシュリスト」, buying immediate comprehension at the cost of the literal singular-word name. Two mechanical warnings: 《》 in Chinese marks titles of works and must not be used for a software feature, and the name must not be re-translated at each of its appearances.

заповедник школоты.finding: One of the two dismissive labels the book itself names (alongside «клон фейсбука») as stuck to VKontakte to avoid explaining it: 'приклеиваемые к нему ярлыки «заповедник школоты» или «клон фейсбука» никак не объясняют этого феномена'. «Заповедник» is a nature reserve or game preserve — a fenced habitat where a species is kept — so the image is of VK as a protected breeding ground for one particular fauna. «Школота» is not neutral 'schoolchildren': it is contemptuous 2000s Runet slang (Lurkmore-era, from imageboards and MMOs) for loud, semi-literate teenage users, applied as an insult to anyone acting immature, and carrying the sneer of 'future быдло'. Said around 2010-2013 by the LiveJournal/Facebook-using older crowd, the phrase meant VK is where the kiddie herd grazes, not a place for serious adults. It is a stock put-down, not the author's own view — he quotes it to reject it.

rendering.en: a game reserve for school brats

заповедник школоты.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a wildlife-reserve full of schoolkids) and the contemptuous register, and each picks the local internet put-down for immature young users rather than the neutral word for pupils: 'school brats' in English, 小学生 in its Chinese online sense of clueless juvenile users, 厨房 in its 2ch sense of 中坊. What is sacrificed is the specific Runet provenance of «школота» — an English, Chinese or Japanese reader will hear their own subculture's sneer, not Lurkmore's — and in Chinese the literal reading 'primary-school pupils' may surface (fallback: “小屁孩保护区”).

гопники.finding: Young working-class men from the outer housing estates: poorly educated, moving in packs, territorial, given to shakedowns and casual violence. The etymology is contested and both branches are Petersburg ones — either the acronym ГОП, the Городское общество призрения poorhouse on Ligovsky prospekt (later Городское общежитие пролетариата), or Dahl's «гоп», a jump or a blow, which also gives «гоп-стоп» for a street mugging; that local origin matters here because Kononov's boy is scanning a Petersburg estate. The peak was the 1990s and early 2000s, exactly the years of Durov's childhood, and the word was already fading by the time the book was written. One trap is chronological: the Adidas-tracksuit, sunflower-seed, 'Slav squat' image only became an international ironic meme after Reddit picked it up around 2012, so a translator who reaches for that iconography in a 1990s scene imports a joke that did not yet exist. The other trap is class: гопник is what the nerd's world calls its natural predator, the opposite pole from «ботаники», and the book needs the two tribes to stay named and opposed.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gopnik
https://scholarship.claremont.edu/pomona_theses/238 (Pomona thesis, 'Gopniki: Peripheral Masculinity in Post-Soviet Russia')

https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%B4%E3%83%97%E3%83%8B%E3%82%AF (ゴプニク is the Japanese headword)

гопники.rationale: I keep the word foreign in all three languages and pay for it with one first-use gloss — 'gopniks, the tracksuited toughs of the estates' / 戈普尼克（gopnik，苏联式住宅区里的街头混混）/ ゴプニク（ロシア版ヤンキー） — because the alternatives all import the wrong country: 'chavs' is Britain, 街头混混 is generic and dissolves the nerd-versus-gopnik opposition the book is built on, and a bare ヤンキー brings 特攻服 and motorbikes with it. What I preserve is denotation, class specificity and the pejorative edge; what I give up is immediate transparency, and in Chinese also settledness, since 戈普尼克 is my coinage rather than an established term and Chinese coverage of the subculture usually just keeps the Latin 'Gopnik' — that is the fallback if the publisher dislikes transliteration.

институты-ящики.finding: From 1927 Soviet defence plants and, after the war, their research institutes and design bureaus (НИИ, КБ) were given open 'conditional' addresses consisting of a city plus a post-box number — 'г. Ленинград, п/я 496' — instead of a name, so the numbered designations were abolished in 1966 and the п/я system formally only in 1989. «Ящик» is therefore a postal box, not a crate, and 'работать в ящике' became everyday shorthand for holding a classified job in the military-industrial or security complex, with a «первый отдел» watching the staff. For a Russian reader the word carries two things at once: secrecy and privilege — the box was closed, unpublishable and travel-restricted, but it was also a sheltered berth with decent conditions and real intellectual work, which is exactly Kononov's point when he says the communists 'hid the nerds' in the post-box institutes and gave them a survivable climate. The trap is twofold: 'box institutes' is meaningless in English, and the institutes must not be confused with the «шарашка», the prison design bureau of Solzhenitsyn's The First Circle — these people were employed, not imprisoned.

Сергей Рукшин.finding: Sergei Evgenyevich Rukshin (b. 10 Nov 1957), the Leningrad/St Petersburg maths-circle coach who started teaching at the Palace of Pioneers in 1975 while still an 18-year-old matmekh undergraduate, took Grigori Perelman from fifth grade onward, and in the early 1990s moved his circle out of the Palace (the administration wanted to charge parents) into Physics-Mathematics Lyceum No. 239 as the free City Mathematics Centre for Gifted Schoolchildren, which he still runs. He is the only teacher in the world to have raised two Fields medallists — Perelman and Stanislav Smirnov — and by 2013 his pupils had taken roughly 90 medals at the International Mathematical Olympiad; in that year he was a Herzen University docent, deputy director for science at Lyceum 239, and, on the Education Ministry's public council, one of the loudest press critics of the reform of Russian schooling (he was named People's Teacher of the Russian Federation only in 2017, after the book). For a Russian reader of 2013 the name is not obscure: after Perelman refused the Millennium Prize in 2010 Rukshin was the man the press went to for comment, so «Рукшин» reads instantly as 'the man who made Perelman', a certificate of authenticity for the Petersburg talent pipeline that produced Nikolai Durov's cohort — the point Kononov is making by naming him. The name carries no irony and no colour of its own; everything it carries is the Perelman link, which is exactly what disappears the moment it crosses a border.

Сергей Рукшин.rationale: All three keep the transliterated name in the forms readers can already match to the Perelman literature — Gessen's Perfect Rigor for English, 鲁克申 as used in Chinese coverage of Perelman (the Chinese edition of Gessen has 鲁克辛, worth a footnote if that book is cited), ルクシン as in the Japanese 『完全なる証明』 — and buy back the lost connotation with a short first-mention apposition, since outside Russia the bare name means nothing. What is sacrificed is compression and the offhand tone of the Russian, where no gloss is needed; a translator should not also unpack his education-reform notoriety, which the book does not use.

нёрды.finding: «Нёрд» is a raw English loan, still marked as foreign in Russian in 2013 (the spelling wobbles between нёрд, нерд and нёрд, and it usually arrives with a gloss). It sits in a three-way system the translator has to keep apart: «ботаник» is the native school word for a swot, a mocking label pinned on someone from outside; «задрот» is coarse and pejorative, an obsessive, often a gamer; «гик» is the other loan, an enthusiast of a niche, socially outward-facing. «Нёрд» is the newest of the four and the only one with no Russian baggage, which is exactly why the Runet press of 2010-2013 used it approvingly for programmers — it imports the American arc in which the nerd stopped being the loser and became the person who owns the industry (Zuckerberg, Gates, The Big Bang Theory), and it can be worn as a self-description, which «ботаник» cannot. Kononov uses it that way: nerds as the class that took the noosphere, not as a sneer. The proposed Chinese 呆客 is not an attested word; the Chinese system also splits three ways, 极客 = geek, 书呆子 = swot/bookworm (the natural «ботаник»), and 技术宅 = the tech nerd, a self-applied label carried by the well-known slogan 技术宅拯救世界 ('tech nerds save the world'), which matches Kononov's thesis closely. Japanese ナード is likewise a conscious import of the American stereotype and is kept distinct from native オタク and ガリ勉, mirroring the Russian situation almost exactly.

https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Гик_(человек) (гик vs нерд in Russian usage)
https://skillbox.ru/media/code/gik-i-nerd/ (Russian tech-press account of nerd shifting from insult to self-description)

нёрды.rationale: English and Japanese keep all three — the loan goes home in English, and ナード is itself a loan that reads as imported American, so the slight foreignness of «нёрды» survives. Chinese trades the foreignness for idiom: 技术宅 is native-looking rather than borrowed, but it is the one attested Chinese label that is self-applied and admiring rather than mocking, leaving 书呆子 free for «ботаник» and 极客 for «гик»; 呆客 should not be used, as it is not a real term.

«Обломов».finding: Goncharov's 1859 novel about a landowner who cannot get off his sofa, and a compulsory text in the Russian school syllabus — which is what the scene turns on: Durov is not discovering the book, he is attacking a set text in front of a class that has been taught to love it. Dobrolyubov's essay «Что такое обломовщина?» made обломовщина a standing Russian word for national sloth, later used by Lenin against bureaucratic inertia, so 'a work that poeticises laziness should be struck from the curriculum' lands as heresy against a shared diagnosis, not as literary criticism. Oblomov's foil is Andrei Stolz, half-German, industrious, mechanical: the class defends the Russian sluggard and dismisses Stolz as «бездушный немчура», and that word is a contemptuous collective for Germans, not the neutral «немец» — flatten it to 'German' and the pupils stop sounding like teenagers. All three target languages have canonical published translations, so the title is a lookup: 人民文学出版社's 《奥勃洛莫夫》 (tr. 陈馥) and Iwanami Bunko's 『オブローモフ』 (tr. 米川正夫).

https://book.douban.com/subject/33451938/ (人民文学出版社 edition, tr. 陈馥)
https://www.iwanami.co.jp/book/b248167.html (岩波文庫『オブローモフ』, tr. 米川正夫)
https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%AA%E3%83%96%E3%83%AD%E3%83%BC%E3%83%A2%E3%83%95 (also gives ドブロリューボフ『オブローモフ主義とは何か？』, tr. 金子幸彦, 岩波文庫 1975)
https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_12749306 (shows the competing Chinese variant 《奥勃洛摩夫》)
«Обломов».rationale: I take the published title in each language, which preserves denotation and lets a reader follow the reference up, and I accept the one loss that cannot be repaired: for a Russian the name arrives pre-loaded from school, whereas an English, Chinese or Japanese reader needs a half-clause of apposition on first mention, and no domestic set text may be substituted for it. Three consistency riders travel with this decision: Stolz is Stolz / 施托尔茨 / シュトルツ, обломовщина is Oblomovism / 奥勃洛莫夫性格 / オブローモフ主義, and in Chinese use 莫 not 摩, since both 《奥勃洛莫夫》 and 《奥勃洛摩夫》 are in circulation; «немчура» should keep its sneer — 'that soulless Kraut' is too Second World War, but 德国佬 and ドイツ野郎 sit at about the right level of schoolboy contempt.

Михаил Мирилашвили.finding: Mikhail Mikhailovich Mirilashvili (b. May 1960), a Georgian-Jewish businessman in St Petersburg and father of VK co-founder Vyacheslav 'Slava' Mirilashvili. He founded the casino corporation «Конти» in 1992, the largest gambling business in the former USSR, and ran «Джекпот», Europe's biggest satellite-linked slot-machine network, until Russia banned gambling in 2009; he also headed the «Петромир» holding, and was vice-president of the Russian Jewish Congress. In January 2001 he was arrested and in 2003 convicted by the Leningrad Military District court of organising the abduction of Rostom Dvali and Koba Kakushadze, the men suspected of kidnapping his own father — acquitted of murder, sentenced to 12 years, cut to 8 by the Supreme Court, released in 2009 — a case that split Petersburg opinion, with actors and deputies picketing in his support and his lawyers calling it fabricated. For a Russian reader of 2013 the name therefore means gambling money plus a notorious criminal case, the shadow the book means when Slava's family sends him abroad; in Israel, where the family later based itself, he is written Mikhael (Michael) Mirilashvili of Watergen. Two traps: «однорукие бандиты» in his business is the ordinary Russian word for slot machines, not human robbers, and three generations here are named Mikhail — the grandfather Mikhail Gabrielovich, this Mikhail, and Slava's own patronymic.

Михаил Мирилашвили.rationale: I keep the Russian-period form of the name in all three languages, since the book's world is Petersburg and not Israel, and add a one-off first-mention gloss so the reader gets the gambling-and-scandal connotation that the bare name carries for Russians; the Israeli spelling is noted only for indexes and cross-references. Nearby «однорукие бандиты» should become the ordinary local word for slot machines — 老虎机 in Chinese, スロットマシン in Japanese — while English can keep 'one-armed bandits', which is the same idiom.

Why Nerds Are Unpopular.finding: Paul Graham's essay, first posted February 2003 at paulgraham.com/nerds.html and reprinted as chapter 1 of Hackers & Painters (O'Reilly, 2004). It argues that clever American schoolchildren are unpopular not because they are disliked but because they are playing a different game: popularity is a full-time job and nerds are spending their attention elsewhere. For a Russian technology reader around 2013 this was close to a subculture password rather than an obscure citation: Graham was the best-known ideologist of the startup world, Y Combinator was already famous, and volunteer Russian translations of his essays circulated widely; the essay's standard Russian title is «Почему ботаники непопулярны». Kononov cites it twice — once with the English title in the prologue, once in Russian translation in chapter 1 — and both times as a ready-made description of the VKontakte crowd, so the two citations must be recognisable as the same text. Crucially, both Chinese and Japanese have published book translations with fixed chapter titles, so this is a lookup, not a translation problem.

Why Nerds Are Unpopular.rationale: In every language I preserve recognisability — the exact wording a reader of that language would find if they went looking — over literal fidelity, and I keep the same title at both citations so the reader sees one essay rather than two. The Japanese cost is real and worth accepting: the published title uses オタク, which carries anime-fandom associations Graham's 'nerd' does not, and もてない narrows 'unpopular' towards 'unpopular with girls', so on first use I would add ポール・グレアムのエッセイ and, where the surrounding sentence leans on the Russian «ботаники», gloss ナード in parentheses; 书呆子 similarly loses the technical affinity of 'nerd' but is what a Chinese programmer has actually read.
